title: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 797. Scope: standard axiom systems of mathematics such as arithmetic, group theory and set theory

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-40: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.44

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Formal corpora and model theory can test particular meanings of completeness and model difference. The broad assertion that widely used theories are usually close to complete is representation-dependent and not settled by any existing corpus.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Choose a formal language and distribution over bounded-length sentences for each named theory, measure the fraction decided, and characterize elementary equivalence and definable differences among standard and nonstandard models. Results test closeness only under that chosen language and weighting.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Proof-corpus frequency confounds truth with research selection.

There is no canonical distribution over mathematical statements.

Nonstandard models can differ profoundly despite elementary equivalence.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.3
data existence: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Model theory and formal libraries give real information: arithmetic decides ordinary number-theoretic statements and its other models are not explicit, while some textbook systems, such as the bare group axioms, decide much less. Fair fraction and usually are not tied to a measure or a closed list of systems. These results test examples rather than the general claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For a standard system, estimate the density of sentences the axioms decide under a stated length measure, and inspect how explicitly other models can be described. A large, easily described set of independent sentences would challenge close to complete; a density near one half on each side of negation would support it for that system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fair fraction and close to complete need a measure on statements.

The raw group axioms are highly incomplete until further axioms pick out a specific group.

Nonstandard models of arithmetic are known to exist and are also non-constructive, so obscure stays a judgment.
